A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same character-knowledge error detection study, 990-query benchmark, and S2RD method. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison despite renaming and expanded evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 14 LLMs, comparisons of S2RD with reasoning baselines, component ablations, evaluator validation, and additional experiments in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds evaluations of seven models and a multi-turn conversation experiment.

M1.justification: S2RD retains self-narrative generation, three seed memories, retrieval, self-doubt, and final inference with examples. Its appendix prompt is unchanged. Renaming the inference function from F to A and testing conversational histories do not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: Section 6.5 extends evaluation from isolated queries to conversations lasting up to four turns, introducing historical erroneous queries as an input condition. This addresses v1's explicit single-turn restriction. The nine characters, four memory categories, two error types, and 990-query dataset remain unchanged under the new name RoleKE-Bench.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds DeepSeek-R1, QwQ-32B, DS-Qwen-32B, DS-Qwen-7B, Baichuan-NPC, MiniMax, and Xingchen-Plus, expanding from 14 to 21 models and introducing a reasoning-model group. The reasoning-method comparators in Table 3 remain unchanged. ERNIE-Char and Mixtral-v0.1 are renamed existing entries.

E3.justification: The new multi-turn protocol evaluates only the final response and applies S2RD only at that turn. Historical queries share the target's character and error type, are retrieved using embedding similarity, and have randomized ordering (Appendix F.3). This substantially extends the single-turn evaluation design; the existing judge and accuracy metric are retained.

E4.justification: New Table 4 tests sensitivity to conversation length for Vanilla and S2RD on Qwen2-7b and LLaMA3-8b. The UKE case study also changes from Socrates to Martin Luther King Jr., now showing successful Few-shot detection. Existing component ablations, t-SNE analyses, and appendix experiments are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report three evaluations with SEM in Table 2 and three-trial average accuracies for the method comparisons. The original models' means and SEMs are identical. Additional model rows follow the existing reporting practice, without new seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds seven models' results, multi-turn accuracy results, and replacement UKE case responses. All original Table 2 scores, Table 3 method and ablation scores, and the supplementary comparison in v1 Table 7/v2 Table 8 are unchanged. New results have reporting inconsistencies: DeepSeek-R1's 60.35% KKE average exceeds every corresponding category score.

T1.justification: Equations 1–3 retain the same mathematical relationships and frozen-parameter formulation; F is renamed A. Appendix A explains existing knowledge-error concepts without introducing mathematical definitions, assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The task, benchmark, and S2RD contributions remain substantively the same. The introduction revises the claimed KKE–UKE accuracy gap from about 20% to about 15%, although the corresponding Section 6.3 heading still says 20%. The headline finding that detection remains difficult is retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking reasoning-model weakness to math/coding-focused training and multi-turn gains to stronger role activation. It replaces the single-turn limitation with the qualification that S2RD does not directly improve native model capability. The revised UKE case discussion acknowledges Few-shot success and emphasizes S2RD's language diversity.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 and Appendix B provide additional segmentation, manual-review, filter-recruitment, and filtering instructions, clarifying the retention percentages. Appendix D and Table 7 disclose decoding settings and expand model-ID/access information; Appendix F.3 documents history retrieval. These details do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: Seven references are added, including DeepSeek-R1, EmoCharacter, CharacterBox, CoSER, and work on reasoning versus role-playing ability. Cao et al.'s personalized-steering paper and Zheng et al.'s MT-Bench judge paper are removed. The overall positioning around reliable automated role-playing corpus construction remains stable.

P1.justification: v2 names the benchmark RoleKE-Bench, expands the title, changes author ordering/contact text, and rewrites portions of task formulation, construction, evaluation, and conclusion. It adds explanatory appendix sections while retaining the main section sequence and much of the original prose.

P2.justification: Table 2 changes from vertically stacked KKE/UKE panels to a combined table with adjacent columns. v2 adds the multi-turn table, expands the model-access table, revises Figure 2 and the case-study display, and adds Tables 9–10 that redisplay existing evaluator prompts. These are substantial changes to the presentation of experimental material.

improvement.justification: Broader model coverage, multi-turn testing, and clearer construction and decoding documentation benefit v2. However, new Table 2 reports DeepSeek-R1's KKE average as 60.35% despite category scores of 42.56–57.49%, and new Table 4 gives Qwen2-7b's first-turn UKE accuracy as 22.49% versus 30.17% in Tables 2–3. With the original experiments unchanged, these unresolved inconsistencies undermine the added evidence and prevent a reliable judgment of net quality improvement.
